How to read these plans: Each lesson has (A) a Teacher Plan with clock times, steps, the listening script, and answer keys, and (B) a Student Page to print. The student page has the listening tasks, grammar box, Spanish note (Nota para hispanohablantes, written for learners to read on their own; teachers don't need to read or explain it), tips for all learners, and the homework. Audio files are in audio/ (L1_listening.mp3 … L13_listening.mp3, plus the exam files Midterm_listening.mp3 and Final_listening.mp3). Each file plays the conversation once; play the audio again if needed. No speaker or device? Read the script aloud with a volunteer learner.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number make one group of 3. New partners: matching cards, or line up by birthday month and "fold" the line. Inside–outside circles: inner circle faces out, outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person clockwise each round. Instruction rule: Model it (show with one learner), check it (ask "Do you write or speak?"), then go (start the timer).

You don't need to speak Spanish. Teach in English. The Spanish notes on the student pages are for learners to read on their own. They are not something you need to read, translate, or explain.

When a learner is stuck or asks something in Spanish: (1) show it: use the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more simple English example; (3) point to the Grammar Box or the Spanish note on their page; (4) ask a classmate to help for a few seconds, then continue in English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Grammar Box 1: Questions with be (am / is / are)

Choose one word from each column. Read across.

Grammar Box 2: Questions with do / does

QUESTION

Doeshe / shelive here? / work at night? / have kids?
→
ANSWER

No,Idon't.

No,he / shedoesn't.

Grammar Box 3: Wh- questions

QUESTION
Whereareyoufrom?
Wheredoyoulive?
Wheredoyouwork?
Whatdoyoudo?
→
ANSWER
I'mfromHonduras. / Colombia. / Mexico.
Iliveon Pine Street. / near the park.
Iworkat a hotel. / at a bakery.
I'macook. / driver. / teacher.

Questions and answers

Q: How do I make a question in English?

A: Put a helper word at the front: am / is / are or do / does.

Q: When do I use am / is / are?

A: With where you're from, age, job title, feelings, married/single, and places. Look at Box 1.

Q: When do I use do / does?

A: With action verbs like live, work, have, like, speak. Look at Box 2.

Q: What order do the words go in?

A: Question word → helper → person → the rest. Look at Box 3.

Q: How do I give a short answer?

A: Use the same helper as the question. Are you…? → Yes, I am. Do you…? → Yes, I do.

Q: Can I use do and are together?

A: No, never. ✗ Do you are married? ✓ Are you married?

Q: How do I say my age?

A: With be: I'm 35. (not I have 35 years)

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Where you are from?Where are you from?
Where you live?Where do you live?
Do you are married?Are you married?
I have 35 years.I'm 35.
Is from Peru.She's from Peru.
Yes, I live.Yes, I do.

Nota para hispanohablantes: En español decimos «¿Dónde vives?» sin palabra extra. En inglés la pregunta necesita do/does o am/is/are al principio: Where do you live? La edad usa be: I'm 35 (no «I have 35 years»). Y siempre usa la persona: She's from Peru (no «Is from Peru»).

Tip for speakers of other languages: If your language makes questions with only your voice, or puts the question word at the end, remember: English needs a helper word (do / are) at the beginning.

Objectives: learners can…

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Welcome + Name Chain · 10 min

  • Grouping: two circles (15 learners) / one circle (7–8 learners).
  • Model: "I'm Ana. I like coffee."
  • Do: each next person repeats the previous person, then adds their own: "She's Ana. She likes coffee. I'm Carlos. I like soccer."
  • Late arrivals: join the circle.
  • If behind: go around once only.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:15 · Orientation: "How Our Class Works" · 5 min

  • Grouping: whole class.
  • Cover: class times and the break; homework every week (short!), checked at the start of class.
  • Language rule: "English in class. If you're stuck, a classmate can help you for a few seconds. Then back to English." You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other. Just smile and say "Now in English, please."
  • Also say: phones are OK for audio and dictionary. "You can tell the truth or make it up."
  • If behind: hand out the sheet and read the 3 key rules only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:23 · New Words · 8 min

  • Grouping: pairs.
  • Do: open the Student Workbook to the New Words page. Point to each picture, say the word; learners repeat twice.
  • Pairs: A points to a picture, B says the word. Then switch.
  • Extra example: show the ID card for a fictional person.
  • If behind: teach only the ★ words.

Step 4 · 6:23–6:33 · Listening + "Say it" · 10 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Before you listen (1 min): "Rosa and Sam meet. What questions do they ask?" Write 2–3 guesses.
  • Listen 1 → Task A (true/false). Listen 2 → Task B (circle). Listen 3 → Task C (write are / do).
  • Pairs compare after each task.
  • "Say it" (1–2 min): pause after "Where are you from?" and "Where do you live?" The class repeats each line twice.
  • Bridge to grammar: "When do we use are? When do we use do?"
  • If behind: skip the third play; do Task C together (teacher reads the 4 lines).

Step 5 · 6:33–6:45 · Grammar: be or do? · 12 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs.
  • Show: the Grammar Box (question side / answer side).
  • Say: "English questions need a helper word at the front. With am/is/are, move it to the front. With no be, borrow do or does."
  • Q&A: a learner reads a Q; the class guesses; read the A; write one example on the board.
  • Check questions: "___ you like rice?" (do) • "___ you tired?" (are) • "Where ___ she work?" (does)
  • Pair check (last 3–4 min): A builds a question from the box; B answers from the answer side.
  • If behind: skip the pair check.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Set up the "Find Someone Who" sheets during the break.

Step 6 · 7:00–7:10 · Talk Time: Find Someone Who · 10 min

  • Grouping: mingle (talk to 6+ people / everyone).
  • Do: learners turn each prompt into a correct question (Do you live near here? / Are you a morning person?).
  • When someone says yes: write their name and ask one follow-up question. One name per row.
  • Baseline snapshot: the teacher (or a second volunteer) uses the checklist: Can they ask a do question? Answer in a full sentence? Give 1 extra detail?
  • Later: formal 2-minute baseline interviews in Weeks 2–3 (about 5 learners per week).
  • If behind: learners talk to 4 people.

Step 7 · 7:10–7:15 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: write one be question and one do question.
  • Homework: explain it from the workbook and do item 1 together.

If time · 7:15–7:30 · pick in this order

  • ① Pronunciation (5 min): Yes/No questions go up ↗; Wh- questions go down ↘. Hum the melody, then say the words. Pairs: A says a question, B draws the arrow in the air.
  • ② Question Scramble (5 min): each pair builds 4 questions from an envelope of word cards.
  • ③ Interview and Introduce (10 min): partners interview each other, then introduce the partner to a group: "This is Marta. She's from Guatemala." (Previews Lesson 2's -s. Don't teach it yet.)

Listening script: L1_listening.mp3 (about 1:10; the conversation plays once, so play the audio again if needed)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer learner.

Narrator: Lesson one. Listening. Rosa and Sam meet at the community center. Listen.

Rosa: Hi! Are you new here?

Sam: Yes, I am. I'm Sam. Nice to meet you.

Rosa: Nice to meet you too. I'm Rosa. Where are you from, Sam?

Sam: I'm from Honduras. And you?

Rosa: I'm from Colombia. Where do you live?

Sam: I live on Pine Street, near the park.

Rosa: Oh, me too! Do you work near here?

Sam: Yes, I do. I work at a hotel. I'm a cook. What do you do?

Rosa: I work at a bakery. I start very early, at five in the morning!

Sam: Wow. Do you have kids?

Rosa: Yes, I do. I have two daughters. Are you married?

Sam: No, I'm not. But my brother lives here with me.

Rosa: That's nice. Well, see you in class!

Sam: See you!

Answer key

  • Task A: 1 T, 2 F (Honduras), 3 T, 4 F (a hotel), 5 T.
  • Task B: 1 a cook, 2 5:00, 3 brother.
  • Task C: 1 are, 2 do, 3 Do, 4 Are.

Teacher notes

  • Privacy: never ask about immigration status, money, or exact addresses. Married/single is optional; Do you have family here? is an alternative.
  • Mixed levels: stronger learners add a follow-up question to every answer; newer learners use the question cards as a script.
  • Typical mistakes from Spanish speakers: I have 35 years (Spanish uses "have" for age) and Where you live? (Spanish questions need no helper word). These are the two most common errors this week. Write the correct form on the board, and point learners to the Spanish note on their Grammar page. They can read it themselves; you don't need to explain it.

Grammar Box 1: Yes/No questions

Choose one word from each column. Read across.

QUESTION
Doyou / theywork? / drive? / cook?
Doeshe / she / itwork? / drive? / cook?
→
ANSWER
Yes,I / we / theydo.
No,I / we / theydon't.
Yes,he / she / itdoes.
No,he / she / itdoesn't.

Answer about yourself: Do you work? → Yes, I do.

Grammar Box 2: What time…? and How often…?

QUESTION
What timedoyouget up? / start work?
What timedoeshe / sheget up? / start work?
How oftendoyoucook? / drive?
How oftendoeshe / shecook? / drive?
→
ANSWER
Iget up / start workat 6:00. / at 7:30.
He / Shegets up / starts workat 6:00. / at 7:30.
Ialways / sometimes / nevercook. / drive.
He / Shealways / sometimes / nevercooks. / drives.

Sentences: positive and negative

Person✔ Positive✘ Negative
I / You / We / TheyI work.I don't work.
He / She / ItShe works.She doesn't work.

Questions and answers

Q: When do I use the simple present?

A: For routines and facts: things that happen again and again. I work at a hospital. I get up at 6.

Q: When do I add -s to the verb?

A: Only with he, she, it (one other person or thing). She works. Marco takes the bus.

Q: How do I spell the -s?

RuleExamples
Most verbs: +swork → works, play → plays
-sh, -ch, -s, -x, -o: +eswatch → watches, go → goes, do → does
consonant + y: -iesstudy → studies
Specialhave → has

Q: After doesn't or does, does the verb keep the -s?

A: No. The "one -s" rule: the -s moves to does. She works. → She doesn't work. → Does she work?

Q: How do I say how often?

always 100%usuallyoftensometimesrarelynever 0%
I always take the bus.She sometimes cooks.He never drives.

Q: Where do always, usually, never… go?

A: Before the main verb: I usually take the bus. But after be: He is always late. Longer phrases go at the end: I cook every day.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
She work at a store.She works at a store.
He doesn't works.He doesn't work.
Does she works?Does she work?
I go always to the park.I always go to the park.
I am work at a restaurant.I work at a restaurant.
He have two kids.He has two kids.

Nota para hispanohablantes: En español el verbo cambia con cada persona (trabajo, trabajas, trabaja). En inglés solo cambia con he/she/it: agrega -s (she works). ¡No olvides la -s! Y no uses am con otro verbo: I work (no «I am work»).

Tip for speakers of other languages: If your language has no verb endings, make a habit: he / she / it = -s. Circle every -s in your homework.

Questions and answers

Q: How strong are these words?

❤❤ love❤ like😐 don't mind👎 don't like✘ hate

Q: What can I say after like, love, hate, don't mind?

A: A thing (pizza, soccer) or an activity (verb + -ing: cooking, dancing).

Q: Why do I add -ing?

A: -ing turns an action into an activity, like a "thing." (I like to cook is also correct, but in this class we practice -ing.)

Q: How do I spell the -ing?

RuleExamples
Most verbs: +ingcook → cooking, play → playing
Silent e: drop itdance → dancing, make → making
Short verb (1 vowel + 1 consonant): double the last letterswim → swimming, shop → shopping

Q: Me too or Me neither?

A: Look at your partner's sentence. Positive (I like…) → Me too. Negative (I don't like…) → Me neither. Look at Box 3.

Q: Where do a lot and very much go?

A: At the end: I like soccer a lot.

Q: How do I talk about something happening right now?

A: Use am / is / are + verb-ing. I'm cooking. She's waiting.

Q: Can I leave out am / is / are?

A: No. ✗ I cooking. ✓ I'm cooking.

Q: What's the difference between I cook and I'm cooking?

A: I cook = every day, a routine. I'm cooking = right now.

RIGHT NOW: am/is/are + -ingEVERY DAY: simple present
I'm cooking right now.I cook every day.
She's working late today.She works at a hotel.

Q: Is What do you do? the same as What are you doing?

A: No! What do you do? = What's your job? What are you doing? = What are you doing right now?

Q: How do I spell the -ing?

A: The same rules as Lesson 3: cook → cooking, make → making, shop → shopping.

✗ Don't say✓ Say

She is work today.She is working today.
What you are doing?What are you doing?

Tip for speakers of other languages: If your language has no special "now" form, remember the formula: am / is / are + verb-ing = happening now.

Sentences: was and were

Person✔ Positive✘ Negative
I / He / She / ItI was busy.I wasn't busy.
You / We / TheyThey were busy.They weren't busy.

Questions and answers

Q: When do I use was and were?

A: They are the past of be. am / is → was. are → were. I'm tired today. → I was tired yesterday.

Q: How do I make other verbs past?

A: Most verbs add -ed: work → worked, clean → cleaned, watch → watched.

Q: Do I add -s for he or she in the past?

A: No. The past is the same for everyone: I worked. She worked. They worked.

Q: How do I spell the -ed?

RuleExamples
Most verbs: +edclean → cleaned, watch → watched
Ends in e: +ddance → danced, live → lived
consonant + y: -iedstudy → studied, try → tried
Short verb (1 vowel + 1 consonant): doublestop → stopped, plan → planned

Q: How do I say the -ed?

A: Three ways. /t/ worked, /d/ played, /ɪd/ visited. You hear an extra syllable only after t or d.

Q: What does What did you do? mean?

A: It asks about activities in the past. Answer with an -ed verb: I cleaned the house. (Lesson 6 explains did.)

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I was clean the house.I cleaned the house.
She were tired.She was tired.
We was busy.We were busy.
Yesterday I work.Yesterday I worked.
I studyed.I studied.
The movie was bored.The movie was boring.

Nota para hispanohablantes: En español «estuve / estaba / fui» → en inglés was (I, he, she, it) o were (you, we, they). Para otros verbos, agrega -ed: I worked, she worked (igual para todos, ¡sin -s!). No uses was con otro verbo: I cleaned (no «I was clean»). Y cuidado: la película es boring (aburrida); la persona está bored (aburrida).

Tip for speakers of other languages: If your language doesn't change the verb for the past, use two signals: a time word and -ed: Yesterday I worked.

Kim: That sounds nice. Was the food good?

Marco: Oh no. And on Sunday?

Sentences: positive and negative

Questions and answers

Q: What is an irregular verb?

A: A verb that doesn't use -ed in the past: go → went, get → got. Learn them like vocabulary.

Q: How do I make a question in the past?

A: Use did at the front: Did you move here? Where did you grow up?

Q: After did or didn't, is the verb past?

A: No. The "one past" rule: did is already past, so the verb is the base form. Did you go? (not went). I didn't go.

Q: Where does ago go?

A: After the time: five years ago, two weeks ago.

Q: Can I use did with was / were?

A: No. Were you nervous? (not Did you were nervous?)

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Did you went to school?Did you go to school?
I didn't went.I didn't go.
I goed to the store.I went to the store.
Ago five years.Five years ago.
She get married in 2020.She got married in 2020.
Did you were nervous?Were you nervous?

Grammar Box 1: How do you get to…?

Choose one word from each column. Read across.

QUESTION

→

Itake the bus. / drive. / walk. / ride my bike.
He / Shetakes the bus. / drives. / walks.

Grammar Box 2: How long does it take?

QUESTION

→

Grammar Box 3: Which is…?

QUESTION
Which isfaster? / cheaper? / more comfortable? / better?
→
ANSWER
The carisfaster / more comfortable / better
The busischeaper / slower / more crowded

Add than: The car is faster than the bus.

How to compare two things

WordRuleExample
short: fast, cheap, slow+erfast → faster than
ends in e: safe, nice+rsafe → safer than
ends in y: easy, busy-iereasy → easier than
short, 1 vowel + 1 consonant: big, hotdouble + erbig → bigger than
long: expensive, comfortablemore + wordmore expensive than
irregulargood → better, bad → worse, far → farther

Questions and answers

Q: How do I compare two things?

A: Short words: add -er. Long words: use more. Then say than: The bus is cheaper than the car.

Q: Can I say more faster?

A: No. Use -er or more, never both: faster, more expensive.

Q: What are the special words?

A: good → better, bad → worse, far → farther.

Q: What does How long does it take? ask?

A: It asks how much time a trip needs. Answer: It takes twenty minutes.

Q: By or on?

A: by bus, by car, by train, by bike, but on foot (= walk).

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
The bus is more cheap.The bus is cheaper.
The car is more faster.The car is faster.
It's bigger that my house.It's bigger than my house.
The bike is more good.The bike is better.
How much time it takes?How long does it take?
I go by foot.I go on foot. / I walk.

Nota para hispanohablantes: «más rápido que» → faster than (palabra corta: -er; no «more fast»). «más cómodo que» → more comfortable than (palabra larga). «que» = than (no «that»). «¿Cuánto tiempo se tarda?» → How long does it take? «a pie» = on foot.

Tip for speakers of other languages: Comparing two things? Look for -er or more and then than.

Q: When do I use the …-est?

Q: Short or long word?

Q: Do I always say the?

Q: How do I ask if a place is near?

A: Is there a bank near here? (one) • Are there any parks near here? (two or more)

Q: What are the special words?

A: good → the best, bad → the worst, far → the farthest.

Q: How much or How many?

Q: Some or any?

Q: What does I'd like mean?

Q: Can I say breads or rices?

Q: How do I say prices?

A: $3.50 = "three fifty" or "three dollars and fifty cents." $24.50 = "twenty-four fifty."

✗ Don't say✓ Say
How many milk?How much milk?
How many money?How much money? / How much is it?

Questions and answers

Q: have or hurt?

Q: Do I need a?

Q: What does should mean?

Q: should + what?

Questions and answers

Q: How do I make going to?

A: am / is / are + going to + base verb: I'm going to visit my mother. She's going to rest.

Q: going to or -ing for the future?

A: Both are OK for plans. -ing is common for fixed plans with a time: I'm working on Saturday.

Q: What's the difference between Would you like to and Do you want to?

A: Same meaning. Would you like to is more polite. Do you want to is friendly.

Q: How do I say no politely?

A: Sorry, I can't. + a reason: I'm working. / I'm visiting my mother. Maybe add Thanks for asking!

Q: What's gonna?

A: Fast speech for going to. Understand it; in writing, use going to.

have to / need to / don't have to

MeaningExample
necessaryI have to pay the bill. She has to work.
necessaryWe need to fill out a form. He needs to call.
not necessary (you can choose)You don't have to pay today. She doesn't have to come.

Questions and answers

Q: What's the difference between have to and need to?

A: Almost the same: something is necessary. I have to pay the bill. I need to pay the bill.

Q: What does don't have to mean?

A: Not necessary. You can choose. You don't have to pay today = you can pay later. It does not mean "you can't."

Q: have to or has to?

A: he / she / it → has to: She has to work. Questions: Does she have to work?

Q: Can you or Could you?

A: Both are requests. Could you is more polite: good for phone calls, offices, and strangers.

Q: What do I say when I don't understand?

A: Could you repeat that, please? Could you speak more slowly? Can you spell that?

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I have to paying.I have to pay.
I must to pay.I have to pay. / I must pay.
She have to work.She has to work.
Could you to help me?Could you help me?
Does she has to go?Does she have to go?
You don't have to smoke here. (= not necessary)You can't smoke here. (= not allowed)

Nota para hispanohablantes: «Tengo que pagar» → I have to pay / I need to pay (con to + verbo base). «No tienes que pagar hoy» → You don't have to pay today = no es necesario (¡no es una prohibición! Prohibido = can't). «¿Podría…?» → Could you…? (más cortés que Can you…?).

Tip for speakers of other languages: On the phone, always keep these phrases ready: Could you repeat that? Can you spell that? Could you speak more slowly?

  • Say: "have to / need to = it is necessary. don't have to = not necessary (you can choose). For requests: Can you…? is friendly; Could you…? is more polite."
  • Board: I have to pay. She has to pay. Do I have to pay? You don't have to pay today.
  • Grammar Boxes + Q&A: learner reads Q → class guesses → read A → board example.
  • Check: "He ___ to work tomorrow." (has) • "Do I have to pay today? — It's due on the 15th." (No, you don't have to) • "Could you to help me?" (Could you help me?)
  • Short "Errand List" (last 5 min): pairs tell 3 things they have to do this week and 1 thing they don't have to do.
  • If behind: skip the "Errand List".

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Arrange chairs back to back for the phone role plays during the break.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:10 · Talk Time: Phone Service Role Plays · 10 min

  • Grouping: Pairs, back to back (15) / pairs + teacher (7–8).
  • Set up: partners sit back to back (like a phone call, no faces).
  • Do: customer card (problem + invented name + account number) and agent card. The agent asks Can you spell that? Could you repeat your account number? The customer writes what they have to do.
  • Switch after 4 minutes with a new card.
  • If behind: one role play only.

Step 6 · 7:10–7:15 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: one sentence with have to or need to and one request with Could you…?
  • Homework: explain it.

If time · 7:15–7:30 · pick in this order

  • ① Pronunciation: "have to" → "hafta" (5 min): have to sounds like "HAF-tuh," has to → "HAS-tuh," Could you → "COOD-juh." Recognize first. Then polite intonation: requests start higher and sound friendly (Could you HELP me, please?); flat requests can sound rude. Pairs repeat 3 requests.
  • ② Voicemail (5 min): learners practice leaving a message: Hi, this is ___. My number is 555-01__. Could you call me back, please? Thank you. Partner writes the name and number.
  • ③ Reading a bill (10 min): pairs read a sample bill (fictional company): What is the account number? How much do you have to pay? When is the due date?

Listening script: L12_listening.mp3 (about 1:31; the conversation plays once, so play the audio again if needed)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer learner.

Voices: Sam, Narrator (reused); Agent (new role, no name, any adult voice). City Phone is an invented company. TTS check: Sam spells L-O-P-E-Z letter by letter; listen to confirm each letter is clear. The account number is read digit by digit.

Narrator: Lesson twelve. Listening. Sam calls City Phone. His phone bill is too high. Listen.

Agent: Thank you for calling City Phone customer service. How can I help you?

Sam: Hi. I have a question about my bill. It's too high.

Agent: I can help with that. Could you give me your account number, please?

Sam: Yes. It's four, seven, two, nine, one, six.

Agent: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?

Sam: Sure. Four, seven, two, nine, one, six.

Agent: Thank you. And what's your last name?

Sam: Lopez.

Agent: Can you spell that, please?

Sam: L. O. P. E. Z.

Agent: Thank you, Mr. Lopez. Let me check. Yes, I see the problem. We charged you two times this month. I'm sorry.

Sam: Okay. Do I have to pay the full bill?

Agent: No, you don't have to. You only need to pay forty-five dollars.

Sam: When do I have to pay?

Agent: You have to pay by the fifteenth.

Sam: Great. Could you send me a new bill, please?

Agent: Of course. Is there anything else?

Sam: No, that's all. Thank you very much.

Answer key

  • Task A: 1 too high; 2 two times; 3 $45; 4 the 15th.
  • Task B: account number 472916; last name L-O-P-E-Z.
  • Task C: repeat; spell; have; send.

Teacher notes

  • Companies, names, and numbers are invented. Use only 555-0100 to 555-0199 phone numbers in materials (reserved for fiction).
  • Privacy: never ask learners for real account numbers, bills, or ID numbers. Role cards give invented ones.
  • Many learners find phone calls the hardest real-life task. Teach the "rescue" phrases: Could you repeat that? Could you speak more slowly? Can you spell that?
  • Typical mistakes from Spanish speakers: I have to paying / I must to pay, and You don't have to understood as "you must not" (Spanish no tienes que can mean either). Write the correct form on the board and point learners to the Spanish note on their Grammar page.

→

Grammar Box 3: Goals and dreams

→

Tense helper

Time wordsTenseExample
ago, last year, yesterdayPastI moved here two years ago. I was nervous.
every day, usually, alwaysPresentI work at a bakery. I take the bus.
now, right now, todayPresent continuousI'm studying English now.
tomorrow, next year, this weekendgoing to (plans)I'm going to take a computer class.
(offers, promises)will (recognize)I'll help you.

Questions and answers

Q: How do I choose the tense?

A: Look at the time word. ago → past. every day → present. now → -ing. next year → going to.

Q: was or did?

A: was / were with adjectives and places: I was nervous. did with other verbs in questions and negatives: Did you study?

Q: How do I talk about a goal?

A: My goal is to + verb: My goal is to get an office job.

Q: Can I mix tenses in one talk?

A: Yes! A good talk goes then → now → next: I was… Now I… Next year I'm going to…

Q: How do I end a talk?

A: Thank you to my teachers and classmates. Thank you for listening.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I am agree.I agree.
One year ago I am nervous.One year ago I was nervous.
Next year I take a class.Next year I'm going to take a class.
In the next year…Next year…
My goal is get a job.My goal is to get a job.
I have 30 years.I'm 30 (years old).

Nota para hispanohablantes: «Estoy de acuerdo» → I agree (sin am). «El próximo año» → next year (sin in the). «Hace un año estaba nerviosa» → One year ago I was nervous. «Mi meta es conseguir…» → My goal is to get… (con to). «Tengo 30 años» → I'm 30.

Tip for speakers of other languages: Before you speak, find the time word. It tells you which tense to use.

lessons.teacher:
At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • talk about the past, present, and future in one conversation
  • choose the correct tense with a time word (ago / now / next year)
  • talk about feelings then and now (I was nervous. Now I feel proud.)
  • prepare and practice a short graduation talk (4–6 sentences)

Materials

  • Student Workbook, Lesson 13
  • tense helper poster (copy the table from the Grammar page)
  • "Then / Now / Next" cards
  • a timer or phone for practice talks
  • L13_listening.mp3 (script below; audio to be produced)
  • Prep time: 20 min.

Key vocabulary (with pictures in the Student Workbook)

in the past, now, in the future, dream, goal, learn, improve, practice, proud, give a talk, graduate, next step.

Clock-time plan

Core = 6:00–6:45 and 7:00–7:15. Everything after 7:15 is optional ("If time").

How to use this plan: the core is 6:00–6:45 and 7:00–7:15. If you fall behind, use the right-hand column. Everything after 7:15 is optional.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 10 min

  • Grouping: Pairs (same partner for both parts).
  • Minutes 0–5 (review Lesson 12): partners ask What do you have to do this week? Do you have to work on Saturday?
  • Minutes 5–10: partners "play" their voicemail (read it). The listener writes the name and number and asks Could you repeat that?
  • Teacher: write 2 corrected sentences on the board.
  • If behind: collect the homework.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:18 · New Words · 8 min

  • Grouping: Pairs.
  • Do: New Words page: point, say, repeat twice.
  • Then, now, or next? Say a sentence (I was nervous. / I'm going to graduate.). Learners point behind (past), down (now), or forward (future).
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:18–6:30 · Listening + "Say it" · 12 min

  • Grouping: Individuals → pairs.
  • Before you listen: "Ana gives a talk at graduation. What does she talk about?" Take 2 guesses.
  • Listen 1 → Task A (then / now / next). Listen 2 → Task B (true/false). Listen 3 → Task C (fill in).
  • "Say it" (1–2 min): the class repeats "One year ago, I was nervous." and "Now I feel proud."
  • If behind: skip the third play; do Task C together.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar: Review of all tenses · 15 min

  • Grouping: Whole class, then pairs.
  • Say: "The time word tells you the tense. ago / last / yesterday → past. now / right now → present continuous. every day / usually → present. tomorrow / next year → going to."
  • Tense helper table: read each row together. Learners make one sentence per row about themselves.
  • Grammar Boxes + Q&A: learner reads Q → class guesses → read A → board example.
  • Check: "Last year I ___ (work) at a hotel." (worked) • "Next year I ___ (take) a class." (am going to take) • "I am agree or I agree?"
  • Short "Time Word Dice" (last 5 min): pairs take a card with a time word and a verb (last year + live) and make a sentence.
  • If behind: skip the "Time Word Dice".

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Put up the tense helper poster during the break.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:10 · Talk Time: Practice Graduation Talks · 10 min

  • Grouping: Groups of 3 (15: 5 groups) / two groups of 3–4 (7–8).
  • Do (3 min): each learner fills in the talk frame on the Homework page: Then / Now / Next / Thank you.
  • Practice (7 min): each learner gives the talk to the group (about 1 minute). Listeners give one compliment and one question (How did you feel? What are you going to study?).
  • Reassure: at graduation, learners can read from their paper, give the talk with a partner, or just say 2 sentences.
  • If behind: learners write the frame only; practice at home.

Step 6 · 7:10–7:15 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: three sentences: one past, one present, one future.
  • Homework: explain it. Remind learners: final next week (Week 15), graduation in Week 16.

If time · 7:15–7:30 · pick in this order

  • ① Pronunciation: sentence stress for talks (5 min): stress the important words: "One year AGO, I was NERVOUS. NOW, I feel PROUD." Pause at each period. Pairs practice their first 2 sentences.
  • ② Then and Now Interview (5 min): pairs ask Where did you live five years ago? Where do you live now? Where are you going to live in five years?
  • ③ Dream Board (10 min): learners draw 3 pictures (then / now / next) and explain them to a small group. Hang them up for graduation.

Listening script: L13_listening.mp3 (about 0:59; the conversation plays once, so play the audio again if needed)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer learner.

Voices: Ana, Narrator (reused).

Narrator: Lesson thirteen. Listening. Ana gives a short talk at graduation. Listen.

Ana: Good evening, everyone. My name is Ana.

Ana: One year ago, I was very nervous. I didn't understand people at the store. I was afraid to talk on the phone.

Ana: Then I started this class. I came to class every week. I practiced a lot with my classmates.

Ana: Now, I work at a bakery. I talk to customers every day. I make my own appointments at the clinic. I feel proud.

Ana: Next year, I am going to take a computer class. My goal is to get an office job. My dream is to help other people learn English.

Ana: Thank you to my teachers and to my classmates. You helped me a lot. Thank you!

Answer key

  • Task A: nervous = then; works at a bakery = now; makes appointments = now; computer class = next; office job = next (goal).
  • Task B: 1 F (she was nervous); 2 T; 3 F (a bakery); 4 T; 5 F (help other people learn English).
  • Task C: was; practiced; work; going.

Teacher notes

  • This lesson reviews all the grammar from Lessons 1–12. No new grammar except will (shown only in the tense helper, for recognition).
  • Graduation talks are optional. Offer three choices: alone, with a partner, or 2 sentences only. Never force a learner to speak in front of guests.
  • Typical mistakes from Spanish speakers: I am agree (Spanish estoy de acuerdo), I have 30 years (age), and In the next year (→ next year). Write the correct form on the board and point learners to the Spanish note on their Grammar page.
